Chapter 4: Balancing Power, Opposition, and the Needs of the People
With the New Deal in motion, Franklin Roosevelt found himself facing a whole new set of challenges. Sure, that first wave of action brought some much-needed relief and a sense of hope—but let’s be honest, the Depression was nowhere near finished. Unemployment was still sky-high, and the economy felt like it could shatter at any moment.
Franklin was stuck right in the middle. On one side, you had business leaders, worried about too much government getting involved. On the other, workers and labor groups, desperate for more support. And then there were the politicians—some of them skeptical about whether Franklin was steering the country in the right direction.
Now, what really set Franklin apart was his pragmatic, personal approach to leadership. He gathered advisors from all walks of life—professors, social workers, business folks—you name it. He wanted different opinions, real debate, and wasn’t afraid to try new things. If something didn’t work? He’d tweak it, or even admit it was a mistake. That kind of flexibility was rare, especially for someone in his position.
But the pushback wasn’t just noise—it was intense. Some in Congress, including people from Franklin’s own party, thought the New Deal was going way too far. The Supreme Court knocked down some of his key programs, claiming the federal government was reaching beyond its limits. Business leaders started throwing around scary words like "socialism," and others accused Franklin of threatening American democracy itself.
Through all this, Franklin kept his focus on ordinary Americans. He traveled across the country, meeting folks in towns and cities who’d lost nearly everything. He listened to stories of hardship, but also of grit and resilience. Seeing all this up close convinced him—even more—that government really could make a positive difference.
One of the biggest fights was over Social Security. Just imagine—the idea of creating a safety net for seniors, people out of work, and those living with disabilities was completely new at the time. Critics warned it would bankrupt the country or make people too dependent on the government. But Franklin saw it another way. He believed that a nation should be judged by how it treats its most vulnerable people. Getting Social Security passed was a major turning point—it wove the idea of looking out for each other right into the fabric of American life.
Franklin’s willingness to shake up the status quo earned him plenty of fans—and just as many enemies. Some folks saw him as a hero; others called him a dangerous radical. The phrase “traitor to his class” got thrown around. Oddly enough, it became both an insult and a badge of honor. It summed up the tension at the heart of his presidency: balancing privilege with responsibility, old traditions with new ideas.
During these turbulent years, Franklin’s partnership with Eleanor grew even stronger. She became his eyes and ears, traveling far and wide, bringing back stories from the people who felt forgotten. Eleanor pushed Franklin to think more deeply about issues like race, gender, and social justice, and thanks to her, the New Deal reached even further.
As the 1930s drew to a close, you could feel the world shifting. Fascism was rising in Europe, war loomed on the horizon, and the scars of the Depression still lingered. Franklin’s ability to adapt, to listen, and to act boldly—well, all of that was about to be tested like never before.
